hero.p1: Next generation · launching end of 2026 · Chromium · Android · Lua 5.4
hero.h12:
The browser that
runs your code.
hero.p3: Lemur is Chromium with a Lua runtime living inside the browser process. Not an extension API — the whole thing: tabs, network, the DevTools Protocol, the native toolbar, every renderer process. Drop a .lua file in, restart, and the browser is yours.
hero.reach: The household desktop-class browser in Indonesia, Vietnam, Brazil, India and the Philippines.
why.h22:
Extensions ask permission.
Scripts just do it.
why.p3: Browser extensions live in a sandbox on the far side of an API designed to keep them out. A Lemur script is code running in the browser process, next to Chromium's own. Same privileges as the browser, because it is the browser.
why.div7: Rewrite response bodies on the fly
why.div10: Put a button on the real toolbar, or replace the bottom bar
why.div13: Dump, restyle or tear out any native View
why.div15: Full Chrome DevTools Protocol on a phone
why.div16: Desktop only, one domain at a time
why.div18: Fetch anything, no CORS, no host permissions
why.div21: Read and write Chromium's own prefs, site permissions and feature flags
why.div23: Run Lua inside every renderer, on real DOM handles
why.div25: Drive other apps, not just the page
why.div30: Sandboxed UGC domain, separate Lua state
features.p3: From the pixels on the toolbar down to the C++ services behind chrome:// pages.
features.p5: Scripts load from files/lua/ at startup. Local scripts get the full standard library — io, os, debug, require. Your device, your rules.
features.p7: Every CDP domain against every tab, iframe, worker and service worker — plus a browser-level target. v8.eval, dom.query, ax.tree, network emulation, geolocation, UA overrides.
features.p9: Persistent themes, a declarative widget tree mounted on nine slots in the real shell, and a scalpel for the native View hierarchy: style, replace, insert, detach, move, on.
features.p11: The complete C-level Lua API of luakit re-implemented on Chromium: widget{} trees mapped to Android views, webview bound to a tab, luakit.register_scheme, sqlite3, regex, soup, stylesheet, timer, download, ipc_channel. An rc.lua written for luakit runs here.
features.p13: Block, redirect, add or strip headers, rewrite response bodies with string replacements. Pattern-matched, per resource type, applied in the browser process before anything renders.
features.p15: One lua_State per renderer process with page, dom_document and dom_element on real V8 handles, a synchronous send-request hook on every subresource, and luakit.register_function to expose Lua to page JavaScript.
features.h316: An automation base for AI agents
features.p17: Observe → act, in three layers and one coordinate system: the page (screenshot, set-of-marks, CDP), the browser shell (ui.dump, ui.find) and other apps through an accessibility service the user turns on once. Deciding is your model's job; agent.run is the loop.
features.p19: Local scripts are yours and run unrestricted. Shared scripts (UGC) run in their own lua_State with safe libraries only — no privileged API, no shared globals, no confused-deputy path back into yours.
features.p21: lemurx.help() prints the whole catalog, lemurx.help("tabs") one module, and lemurx.catalog is the same list as a table. lemurx.ui.dump() shows the native view tree, lemurx.cdp.targets() every DevTools target. You never have to read our source.
code.p3: Each of these is a complete file. Save it to files/lua/, restart Lemur, done.
architecture.p3: One Lua thread, one JSON protocol in each direction, and every Chromium layer on the other side of it.
architecture.span16: UI · skins · widgets · menu · intents · accessibility service
architecture.span18: prefs · permissions · cookies · history · net rules · custom schemes · renderer Lua
architecture.span20: DevToolsAgentHost per tab / frame / worker / browser
architecture.span23: the Lua runtime lives here, on a single sequenced thread
architecture.p25: All scripts run on one sequenced thread. UI work is posted to the UI thread and awaited. Java callbacks that need a return value are refused instantly when Lua is busy — no UI↔Lua deadlock, ever.
architecture.p27: Every hook added to Chromium — URL-loader and navigation throttles, certificate override, custom schemes, back press, app menu, renderer Lua — is gated on state that only a script can create. With no script running each hook is an early return and the browser behaves like the official build it was compiled from.
architecture.p29: The three-dot menu always ends with a plain Android switch for the Lua runtime that no Lua API can reach or hide. If the process dies twice within 20 s of starting scripts, the runtime disables itself and the browser comes up stock — a script can never lock you out of the browser you need to fix it.
scripts.p3: Anything in files/lua/ugc/ is a shared script: it gets the browser-facing API — tabs, network rules, HTTP, UI widgets, storage — and nothing that could read your cookies, history, or reach the DevTools Protocol. Each one runs in its own Lua state, so it can't touch your globals or ride your privileged callbacks.
scripts.li6: fs jailed to lua/ugc, http.fetch capped at 2 MB / 20 s
scripts.li7: lemurx.ugc.scan(src) lints for forbidden calls before you publish
scripts.li8: Local scripts can expose() a curated function for UGC to import()
extensions.p3: Lemur runs the same extension engine as desktop Chromium. Install straight from the Chrome Web Store or Edge Add-ons, drop in your userscripts, and keep the setup you've spent years tuning — on a phone.
extensions.span5: Manifest V2 & V3, one tap to install
extensions.span7: Same CRX format, same permissions model
extensions.span9: Tampermonkey, Violentmonkey, Greasy Fork — or plain Lua
extensions.p19: Extensions get their own toolbar slot, popups render as bottom sheets, and Lua can talk to them — lemurx.ui.render("toolbar.end", …) sits right next to their icons.
roblox.p1: Roblox power users
roblox.h22:
The metaverse,
with the pro tools on.
roblox.p3: A huge share of Lemur's community lives on Roblox — and they refuse to trade without their extensions. RoPro, BTRoblox and Roblox+ run on Lemur exactly as they do on desktop: try outfits on your avatar before you buy, watch limited-item prices, get trade notifications, and flip items from the phone in your pocket.
roblox.li7: Desktop-mode Roblox pages that stay in desktop mode — per-site, remembered
roblox.li8: Extension popups as bottom sheets, thumb-reachable
roblox.li9: Write your own price alerts in ten lines of Lua with lemurx.timer + lemurx.http
freedom.h22:
The most customizable
mobile browser on Earth.
freedom.p3: Every other mobile browser gives you a theme picker. Lemur gives you the toolbar, the tab strip, the gestures, the network stack and the rendering pipeline — and a scripting language to rewire them. If you can describe it, you can ship it to yourself tonight.
freedom.span5: Persistent themes, per-site overrides, your own widget tree in the shell
freedom.span7: Chrome, Edge, userscripts — thousands of them, unmodified
freedom.span9: Full browser-process access, Lua in every renderer, luakit widgets on real Android views
freedom.span11: Back-gesture, omnibox, downloads, UA, headers: all interceptable
engine.p3: Customization is worthless on a stale engine. Lemur rebases onto each new Chromium stable so the security patches, V8 speedups and web-platform features land in your hands when they land in Chrome's.
engine.p5: Upstream site isolation, sandboxing and the same-day security fixes Chromium ships. Lemur's additions live beside Chromium's code, not on top of a fork that drifts.
engine.p7: Current V8, Skia and the latest Android graphics path. Lua runs on its own thread and never touches the render pipeline unless you tell it to.
engine.p9: No account required, no tracking baked in. Block at the network layer, strip headers, kill third-party cookies — and audit every rule from Lua, because the rules are yours.
sync.h22:
Bookmarks. Extensions. Scripts.
Everywhere you are.
sync.p3: Sign in once and your Lemur follows you. New phone? Restore the toolbar you built, the extensions you trust and the Lua scripts you wrote — in the order you installed them, with their settings.
sync.li4: Bookmarks & reading list — the usual, plus folder order and favicons
sync.li5: Extensions — IDs, enabled state, per-extension options where the extension allows it
sync.li6: Lua scripts — files/lua/ as a versioned bundle; roll back any script to any previous version
sync.li7: Sync is opt-in per category; scripts flagged -- @nosync stay on the device
kiwi.p3: Kiwi Browser proved that a phone browser could run real extensions — then, in January 2025, its founder archived the project after nearly seven years of solo maintenance. The idea was too good to let die. Lemur carries it forward as a commercial, closed-source browser that opens as much as it possibly can through Lua: extension-first, scriptable to the native layers, built so that what you need actually comes true.
kiwi.blockquote4: "I just wanted extensions on mobile for myself." <cite>— Arnaud Granal, on why Kiwi existed</cite>
kiwi.li5: Kiwi users: your extensions install the same way, your bookmarks import in one tap
kiwi.li6: Closed source, open to you: every layer we can expose through Lua, we do — and we keep pushing that line
kiwi.li7: More open, more free, more extensible: the three words we measure every release against
kiwi.p8: If you're a hacker, Lemur was built for you.
community.h22:
Build it. Share it.
Watch it spread.
community.p3: Lemur's UGC community is one place for every kind of add-on: browser extensions, userscripts, and Lua scripts that reach all the way down into the native layers. Publish with one tap, fork anyone's work, remix it, and ship it back. The freedom to create is what turned a browser into a movement.
community.span5: CRX packages, curated collections, one-tap install
community.span9: Skins, HUDs, network rules, deep native tweaks
community.li10: Every shared Lua script runs sandboxed in its own state — creators get freedom, users keep safety
community.li11: Versioned publishing, forks and changelogs; roll back any install to any version
community.li12: Ratings, comments and collections surface the best ideas; lemurx.ugc.scan() lints before you publish
community.li13: Local scripts can expose() curated APIs for community scripts to build on
paip.h22:
UGC powered by Paip.AI.
One shared ecosystem.
paip.p3: Paip.AI is the interest-based social app the founding team built between 2024 and 2026 — real people, real posts, and smart matching that finds friends on your wavelength. Lemur's UGC community runs on Paip.AI's technology and shares one ecosystem with it: one identity, one creator profile, one feed where a Lua script, a skin or an extension collection travels as naturally as a post.
paip.li4: Publish a script in Lemur and it lands on your Paip.AI profile — followers, likes and comments carry over
paip.li5: Interest matching recommends scripts and skins from creators on your wavelength, not just the most downloaded
paip.li6: One account for both: sign in to Lemur with Paip.AI and your UGC library follows you
story.h22:
Six years. Five million geeks.
One browser that answers to you.
story.p3: Lemur was born in 2020 with a stubborn idea: the person holding the phone should have the final say over the software on it. Six years later, five million power users across the world make Lemur their first choice — not because it's the prettiest browser, but because it's the only one that does exactly what they tell it to.
story.span8: Lemur ships: a Chromium for Android that runs Chrome extensions, when almost nothing else on mobile did.
story.span9: Desktop mode, per-site skins, ad and tracker blocking at the network layer. The Roblox community arrives and never leaves.
story.span10: On 6 March, Kevinlinpr steps down as CEO and the founding team leaves to build Paip.AI, an interest-based social app.
story.span11: Kiwi Browser is archived. Lemur commits to keeping mobile extensions alive and open.
story.span12: On 6 September, Kevinlinpr buys back 100% of the company and retakes the helm — and makes the boldest call in Lemur's history: a Lua runtime inside the browser process, with every native layer open to it. The next-generation Lemur launches at the end of 2026.
story.p14: On 6 March 2024, Kevinlinpr stepped down as CEO and the founding team left the company to build Paip.AI, an interest-based social app. On 6 September 2026, Kevinlinpr bought back 100% of the company and returned to take charge of Lemur's future. The brief is simple: open every layer, ship on the latest Chromium, and never make a decision the user can't override. The freedom we promised six years ago is about to get a lot bigger.
docs.p5: Five-minute start, threading model, the two trust domains, every module with examples, recipes, pitfalls, UGC publishing rules.
docs.p9: The same list lemurx.help() prints, rendered: tabs, net, cdp, ui, agent, the luakit layer, the renderer classes and the rest.
docs.p13: Per-site skins, reader mode, desktop-mode memory, back-gesture guard, redirect-page skipping, cross-origin scraping into a floating panel.
download.p2: Next-generation Lemur arrives end of 2026. The current Lemur Browser is on Google Play today.
download.p3: Android 8.0 or newer · arm64 · latest Chromium stable · Lua 5.4.7 · Chrome & Edge extensions · userscripts
download.a4: Get it on Google Play
download.p6: Then drop a .lua file into the app's files/lua/ directory, restart, and watch lemurx.help() print the whole API in logcat.
